slides.heading: The Mughal Empire: sources, rulers and Babur
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we know about the Mughals, who ruled and in what order, and how Babur began the empire.

slides.narration: In this part we learn how historians know about the Mughal Empire. We study a famous book of Akbar's reign and three monuments of Shah Jahan. Then we put the rulers in order and study the three battles of Babur.

The third part of the Akbarnama, completed about 1598

visual.alt: Table about the Ain-i-Akbari: written by Abul Fazl, third part of the Akbarnama completed about 1598, describing administration, revenue, mansabdari, army, provinces, society and statistics of produce and prices

slides.narration: The Ain i Akbari was written by Abul Fazl, a courtier of Akbar. It is the third part of the Akbarnama, completed about fifteen ninety eight. It describes the administration, the revenue system, the mansabdari system, the army, the provinces, society, and statistics of produce and prices.

slides.heading: Value and care
bullets: Value: **detailed official information**.
Care: written by a **courtier**, so it **praises Akbar**.
Compare it with **other sources**.

rows: Written by a courtier, so it praises Akbar
Do not accept every claim as final

visual.alt: Table of the value of the Ain-i-Akbari, detailed official information, and the care needed, since it was written by a courtier who praises Akbar and should be compared with other sources

slides.narration: The book is valuable because it gives detailed official information about the empire. The care needed is that its author was a courtier, so he praises his ruler. A good historian compares it with other sources and does not accept every claim as final.

slides.heading: The Taj Mahal, Agra
bullets: Built by **Shah Jahan** in memory of **Mumtaz Mahal**, about **1632 to 1653**.
**White marble** with inlay of coloured stones, called **pietra dura**.
**Charbagh** garden, **raised platform**, **symmetry**, **double dome**, **four minarets**.
**UNESCO** World Heritage Site, **1983**.

rows: Shah Jahan, in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal
White marble; inlay of coloured stones (pietra dura)

visual.alt: Table of features of the Taj Mahal: built by Shah Jahan in memory of Mumtaz Mahal about 1632 to 1653, white marble with pietra dura inlay, charbagh garden, raised platform, symmetry, double dome, four minarets, World Heritage Site in 1983

slides.narration: The Taj Mahal at Agra was built by Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, about sixteen thirty two to sixteen fifty three. It is of white marble with inlay of coloured stones. It has a four part garden, a raised platform, a double dome and four minarets. It became a World Heritage Site in nineteen eighty three.

slides.heading: The Jama Masjid and the Red Fort, Delhi
bullets: **Jama Masjid**: about **1650 to 1656**; red sandstone and white marble; large **courtyard**; **three domes**, **two minarets**.
**Red Fort**: about **1639 to 1648**; red sandstone walls; **Diwan-i-Am** and **Diwan-i-Khas**.
The Fort stands in his new city, **Shahjahanabad**; a **World Heritage Site** since **2007**.

rows: Red sandstone and white marble; large courtyard; three domes and two minarets; one of the largest mosques in India
Red sandstone walls; Diwan-i-Am and Diwan-i-Khas; in Shahjahanabad; World Heritage Site, 2007

visual.alt: Table of the Jama Masjid built about 1650 to 1656 with a large courtyard, three domes and two minarets, and the Red Fort built about 1639 to 1648 with red sandstone walls and two halls of audience in Shahjahanabad

slides.narration: Shah Jahan also built the Jama Masjid in Delhi, about sixteen fifty to sixteen fifty six. It has a very large courtyard, three domes and two minarets. The Red Fort was built about sixteen thirty nine to sixteen forty eight in his new city, Shahjahanabad. It has red sandstone walls, and the halls of public and private audience. Today the Prime Minister addresses the nation from it on Independence Day.

slides.narration: The Diwan i Am was the hall of public audience, where ordinary petitioners came. The Diwan i Khas was the hall of private audience, for nobles and officers by invitation. Remember am for all and khas for special.

slides.heading: What the monuments reveal
slides.body_md: Read a monument as a source, not only as a sight.

rows: Large buildings of marble and sandstone
A blend of Persian and Indian styles

visual.alt: Table of what the monuments reveal: large buildings show wealth, grand scale shows power, domes and arches show a blend of Persian and Indian styles, and fine work shows skilled craftsmen

slides.narration: Large buildings of marble and sandstone reveal the wealth of the empire. Their grand scale shows the power of the emperor. The domes, arches and inlay show a blend of Persian and Indian styles. The fine work shows skilled craftsmen. One building, however, cannot show the whole empire.

bullets: Against **Ibrahim Lodi**, the last Sultan of Delhi.

slides.narration: At the First Battle of Panipat in fifteen twenty six, Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi. Babur used artillery, a flanking tactic called the tulughma, and defences made of carts. The result was the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the start of Mughal rule.

sections.heading: 1. The Ain-i-Akbari as a source
sections.body_md:
- The **Ain-i-Akbari** was written by **Abul Fazl**, a courtier of Akbar.
- It forms the **third part of the Akbarnama**, which was completed about **1598**.
- It describes the administration, the revenue system, the mansabdari system, the army, the provinces, society and statistics of produce and prices.
- **Value:** it supplies detailed official information on many subjects.
- **Care:** its author served Akbar, so the work praises him; a historian checks its claims against other sources.

sections.heading: 2. Monuments of Shah Jahan
sections.body_md:
- **Taj Mahal, Agra:** built by Shah Jahan in memory of his wife **Mumtaz Mahal**, about **1632 to 1653**. White marble; inlay of coloured stones (**pietra dura**); a **charbagh** (four-part garden); a **double dome**; **four minarets**; a raised platform; symmetry. **UNESCO World Heritage Site, 1983**.
- **Jama Masjid, Delhi:** about **1650 to 1656**; red sandstone and white marble; a large courtyard; **three domes** and **two minarets**; one of the largest mosques in India.
- **Red Fort (Lal Qila), Delhi:** about **1639 to 1648**, in his new city **Shahjahanabad**; red sandstone walls; the **Diwan-i-Am** (hall of public audience) and the **Diwan-i-Khas** (hall of private audience); **World Heritage Site, 2007**. The Prime Minister addresses the nation from it on Independence Day.
- **What they reveal:** wealth, power, a blend of Persian and Indian styles, and skilled craftsmen.

sections.heading: 3. The Mughal rulers in order
sections.body_md:
- **Babur:** about 1526 to 1530.
- **Humayun:** about 1530 to 1540 and 1555 to 1556; his rule was interrupted by **Sher Shah Suri**.
- **Akbar:** about 1556 to 1605.
- **Jahangir:** about 1605 to 1627.
- **Shah Jahan:** about 1628 to 1658.
- **Aurangzeb:** about 1658 to 1707.
- Reign lengths from these years: Babur about 4, Jahangir about 22, Shah Jahan about 30, Akbar about 49 years.

key_terms.definition_md: The dynasty founded by Babur in 1526.
The years in which a ruler rules.

sections.heading: 4. Babur: the three battles
sections.body_md:
- **First Battle of Panipat, 1526:** Babur against **Ibrahim Lodi**. Babur's advantages were **artillery (guns)**, the **tulughma** flanking tactic and **defences of carts**. Result: the **end of the Delhi Sultanate** and the start of Mughal rule.
- **Battle of Khanwa, 1527:** against **Rana Sanga of Mewar** and allies. Result: **Mughal power secured in north India**.
- **Battle of Ghaghra, 1529:** against **Afghan chiefs of Bihar and Bengal**, including **Mahmud Lodi**. Result: **eastern Afghan resistance checked**.

A flanking tactic in which wings swing round the enemy.
Rule over a ruler who keeps his own kingdom.

sections.heading: 5. Akbar: Rajput policy and integration
sections.body_md:
- **Rajput policy:** alliances through marriage (for example with the Kachhwaha ruler of **Amber**, **1562**); **high mansabs** to Rajput nobles (for example **Raja Man Singh**); rulers who accepted Mughal overlordship **kept their kingdoms**; those who refused faced war. **Mewar under Maharana Pratap** resisted, and the **Battle of Haldighati** was fought in **1576**. Aims: a stable empire with loyal allies.
- **Integration:** **Sulh-i-kul** ("peace with all", tolerance); the **pilgrim tax** abolished about **1563** and the **jizya** about **1564**; the **Ibadat Khana** at Fatehpur Sikri (from about **1575**), where scholars of different faiths discussed ideas; **Persian** the language of administration; a **uniform administration**.
- **Din-i-Ilahi** was optional; it had a small following and ended with him.

sections.heading: 6. Akbar: social and educational reforms
sections.body_md:
- **Social reforms (as commonly taught):** forced **sati** discouraged; **widow remarriage** allowed; **child marriage** discouraged by fixing **minimum ages** for marriage.
- **Education:** practical subjects such as **mathematics, agriculture and history** encouraged in schools.
- **Translation department:** Sanskrit works such as the **Mahabharata** were put into Persian (the **Razmnama**), along with other works.
- **Patronage:** scholars, painters and musicians, for example **Tansen**.

sections.heading: 7. The mansabdari system
sections.body_md:
- **Mansab** means **rank**. The system was introduced by **Akbar**, about the **1570s** (dates vary).
- **Zat:** personal rank and pay. **Sawar:** the number of horsemen to be maintained.
- **Ranks** ranged from **10 up to 5,000** for nobles; higher for princes.
- **Payment** was in cash or by a **jagir** (an assignment of land revenue).
- **Rules:** ranks were **not hereditary**; officers were **transferred**.
- **Merits:** an efficient army and administration; loyalty to the emperor; ranks given on merit.
- **Defects:** false musters; pressure on peasants by jagirdars; later a shortage of jagirs and weak control under later rulers.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about, or mixing the order of the six rulers.
- Writing that Humayun ruled in one block; his rule was interrupted by Sher Shah Suri.
- Mixing up the battles and their opponents: Ibrahim Lodi (Panipat), Rana Sanga (Khanwa), Afghan chiefs of the east (Ghaghra).
- Writing zat and sawar the wrong way round: zat is personal rank and pay, sawar is the number of horsemen.
- Giving the Rajput policy without its aim, or describing it in loaded words; use neutral, factual words and describe aims and results.
- Giving only merits or only defects of the mansabdari system.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a result, a link or an assessment.

questions.stem_md: A card in the imagined Hind Reading Room says that a Persian work on the administration of Akbar was written by one of his courtiers. Who wrote the Ain-i-Akbari?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Abul Fazl. Abul Fazl, a courtier of Akbar, wrote the Ain-i-Akbari. Ziauddin Barani wrote a chronicle of the Delhi Sultanate, Tansen was a musician and Raja Man Singh was a noble in Akbar's service.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined history club of Lakshmi Nagar School, Zoya says: "Because the Ain-i-Akbari is so detailed, every line of it must be accepted as the plain truth about Akbar." What is the best reply?

options.text_md: It should be ignored, because a work by a courtier can have no value at all
It should be accepted without checking, because it is a third part of a famous work
It is useful only for the study of the Taj Mahal
It gives detailed official information, but its author was a courtier of Akbar, so its praise should be checked against other sources

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It gives detailed official information, but its author was a courtier of Akbar, so its praise should be checked against other sources. A source is judged by what it offers and by who wrote it. The work is valuable for its detail, yet a courtier tends to praise his ruler, so a historian compares it with other evidence. Rejecting it entirely or accepting it blindly are both poor methods, and it says nothing about the Taj Mahal.

questions.stem_md: Mr. Ilyas, an imagined guide at Agra, tells his group that the white marble tomb behind him was built about 1632 to 1653 in memory of Mumtaz Mahal. Which emperor built it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Shah Jahan. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Akbar, Jahangir and Babur ruled in other periods and are not its builder.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Daryaganj Tours drafts a leaflet on the Taj Mahal. One line in it is mistaken. Which line should be corrected?

options.text_md: It stands on a raised platform with a symmetrical plan
It has a double dome and four minarets
It has three domes and two minarets
It is set in a charbagh, a garden in four parts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It has three domes and two minarets. The first line is mistaken: the Taj Mahal has a double dome and four minarets, while three domes and two minarets describe the Jama Masjid of Delhi. The platform, the symmetry and the charbagh garden are true features of the Taj Mahal.

questions.stem_md: An imagined art class in Delhi sketches a mosque of red sandstone and white marble with a very large courtyard, three domes and two minarets, built by Shah Jahan about 1650 to 1656. Which monument is it?

options.text_md: The tomb of Mumtaz Mahal at Agra

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Jama Masjid, Delhi. The description fits the Jama Masjid of Delhi. The Taj Mahal is a white marble tomb with four minarets, and the Red Fort is a fort with red sandstone walls, not a mosque.

questions.stem_md: The imagined audio guide at the Red Fort says: "You are now entering the hall where the emperor received ordinary petitioners and held open court." Which hall is meant?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Diwan-i-Am. The Diwan-i-Am was the hall of public audience. The Diwan-i-Khas was the hall of private audience, the charbagh is the four-part garden of the Taj Mahal, and the Jama Masjid is a separate mosque.

questions.stem_md: A student at the imagined Sector 9 Public School studies the Taj Mahal, the Jama Masjid and the Red Fort together. Which conclusion do the three monuments best support?

options.text_md: The Mughals built only in white marble and never used red sandstone
All three were built within the reign of a single earlier ruler, Akbar
The monuments show that no other building tradition existed in India
The Mughals had great wealth and power, blended Persian and Indian styles, and employed skilled craftsmen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Mughals had great wealth and power, blended Persian and Indian styles, and employed skilled craftsmen. Large, finely finished buildings point to wealth, power and skilled craftsmen, and their domes, arches and inlay show a blend of Persian and Indian styles. Red sandstone was used at the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid, all three were built under Shah Jahan, and the monuments say nothing about other traditions.

questions.stem_md: An imagined quiz at the Chandni Chowk Heritage Club asks in which year the Red Fort of Delhi was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Which answer is right?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 2007. The Red Fort was listed in 2007. The year 1983 is the listing of the Taj Mahal, 1993 is the listing of the Qutb Minar site, and 1947 is not a listing year at all.

questions.stem_md: A timeline card prepared by the imagined student Ravi shows Akbar (1556 to 1605) and then Shah Jahan (1628 to 1658), with a gap between them. Which ruler fills the gap?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Jahangir. Jahangir ruled about 1605 to 1627, between Akbar and Shah Jahan. Humayun and Babur came before Akbar, and Aurangzeb came after Shah Jahan.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined quiz at Ramnagar School, Neha says that the years of Humayun cannot be written as one block. Why?

options.text_md: He ruled for two empires at the same time
His rule was interrupted by Sher Shah Suri, so it is given as about 1530 to 1540 and again 1555 to 1556
He ruled only after Akbar, from 1556 to 1605
He ruled from 1526 to 1530 and gave way to Akbar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** His rule was interrupted by Sher Shah Suri, so it is given as about 1530 to 1540 and again 1555 to 1556. Humayun lost power to Sher Shah Suri, so his reign is divided into about 1530 to 1540 and 1555 to 1556. The years 1526 to 1530 belong to Babur and 1556 to 1605 to Akbar, and he did not rule two empires at once.

questions.stem_md: The imagined project group of Class IX at Vivek Vidyalaya compares the reigns of Babur (1526 to 1530), Akbar (1556 to 1605), Jahangir (1605 to 1627) and Shah Jahan (1628 to 1658). Which emperor had the shortest reign, and about how long was it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Babur, about 4 years. Subtracting the years gives Babur about 4, Jahangir about 22, Shah Jahan about 30 and Akbar about 49 years. So Babur had the shortest reign of the four, and the other options are longer reigns.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Panipat Gallery displays a diagram with guns at the centre, rows of carts in front of the guns, and wings of cavalry curving round the flanks of the enemy. Which set of advantages of Babur does it show at the First Battle of Panipat?

options.text_md: A large navy, forts on the coast and elephants in the front line
Mountain passes, a siege tower and a supply of silver coins
Only a much larger infantry with no new tactics
Artillery, defences of carts and the tulughma flanking tactic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Artillery, defences of carts and the tulughma flanking tactic. The guns, the carts and the curving wings match Babur's artillery, his defences of carts and the tulughma flanking tactic. A navy and coastal forts are not part of this battle, nor are siege towers, and the battle was not won by numbers alone.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Class IX teacher Mrs. Pillai writes on the board: "1526, defeat of Ibrahim Lodi." What was the main result of this First Battle of Panipat?

options.text_md: The Mughals lost Delhi to the Rajputs
Akbar became the emperor of Hindustan
The eastern Afghan chiefs were checked
The Delhi Sultanate ended and Mughal rule began

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Delhi Sultanate ended and Mughal rule began. The defeat of the last Sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, ended the Delhi Sultanate and began Mughal rule. Akbar came to the throne in 1556, and checking the eastern Afghan chiefs was the result of Ghaghra in 1529.

questions.stem_md: A label in the imagined Rajputana Gallery reads "1527, near Agra: Babur against a Mewar-led alliance under Rana Sanga." Which battle does it describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Battle of Khanwa. The Battle of Khanwa in 1527 was fought against Rana Sanga of Mewar and his allies. Panipat was in 1526 against Ibrahim Lodi, Ghaghra was in 1529 against Afghan chiefs, and Haldighati was in 1576.

questions.stem_md: Four imagined students describe the Battle of Ghaghra in their notes. Whose note is correct?

options.text_md: It was fought in 1526 against Ibrahim Lodi and ended the Sultanate
It was fought in 1529 against Afghan chiefs of Bihar and Bengal, including Mahmud Lodi, and checked eastern Afghan resistance
It was fought in 1527 against Rana Sanga and secured north India
It was fought in 1576 and was the end of Mewar's resistance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It was fought in 1529 against Afghan chiefs of Bihar and Bengal, including Mahmud Lodi, and checked eastern Afghan resistance. Ghaghra took place in 1529 against Afghan chiefs of Bihar and Bengal and checked the eastern Afghan resistance. The other notes describe Panipat, Khanwa and Haldighati, each with its own year.

questions.stem_md: The imagined history teacher Mr. Qadir asks: "If Panipat gave Babur the throne of Delhi, why were Khanwa and Ghaghra still needed?" Which answer is the best explanation?

options.text_md: Panipat ended Lodi rule, but the Mewar-led alliance and the Afghan chiefs of the east remained to be dealt with, so Khanwa secured north India and Ghaghra checked eastern resistance
Panipat was a defeat for Babur, so he had to fight again
Khanwa and Ghaghra were fought only to win the artillery of the enemy
Panipat took place after both battles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Panipat ended Lodi rule, but the Mewar-led alliance and the Afghan chiefs of the east remained to be dealt with, so Khanwa secured north India and Ghaghra checked eastern resistance. Winning at Panipat did not remove every rival. Khanwa in 1527 secured Mughal power in north India and Ghaghra in 1529 checked the Afghan chiefs of the east. Panipat was a Mughal victory in 1526, before the other two battles.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Amber Fort guide Mr. Dev says: "In 1562 a marriage alliance joined the ruling house here with the emperor's family." Which ruling family and which emperor does he mean?

options.text_md: The Sisodia ruler of Mewar and Akbar
The Kachhwaha ruler of Amber and Akbar
The Kachhwaha ruler of Amber and Shah Jahan
The Lodi ruler of Delhi and Babur

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Kachhwaha ruler of Amber and Akbar. Akbar's marriage alliance of 1562 was with the Kachhwaha ruler of Amber. Mewar under Maharana Pratap resisted rather than joined, and Shah Jahan, the Lodis and Babur are not linked with this alliance.

questions.stem_md: Three imagined Rajput rulers, Raja Veer, Rao Madan and Rana Kumar, are shown in a school role-play on Akbar's Rajput policy. Raja Veer accepts Mughal overlordship and is allowed to keep his kingdom. According to the policy, what is likely to happen to a ruler who refuses overlordship?

options.text_md: He is made a mansabdar at once
He is given a larger kingdom
He is asked to move to Fatehpur Sikri
He faces war with the Mughals, as in the Battle of Haldighati in 1576

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** He faces war with the Mughals, as in the Battle of Haldighati in 1576. Rulers who accepted overlordship kept their kingdoms, while those who refused faced war. Mewar under Maharana Pratap resisted, and Haldighati was fought in 1576. A mansab and larger lands were offered to rulers who joined, not to those who refused.

questions.stem_md: A page from the imagined ledger of the Fatehpur village clerk Dinesh notes two taxes that "no longer have to be collected", one dropped about 1563 and the other about 1564. Which two taxes does the clerk mean?

options.text_md: The pilgrim tax and the jizya
The land revenue and the market toll
The jagir tax and the cash tax
The zat tax and the sawar tax

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The pilgrim tax and the jizya. The pilgrim tax was abolished about 1563 and the jizya about 1564. Land revenue continued, and zat and sawar are ranks of mansabdars, not taxes.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined heritage trail of Fatehpur Sikri, a plaque says that from about 1575 scholars of different faiths met in a hall to discuss ideas. What was the hall called?

options.text_md: The Diwan-i-Khas of the Red Fort

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Ibadat Khana. The Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri was the place where scholars of different faiths discussed ideas. The Diwan-i-Khas is in the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid is a mosque and the Razmnama is a translation.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Class IX student Farida lists Akbar's Rajput alliances, the abolition of the pilgrim tax and jizya, the use of Persian in administration and a uniform administration. What aim do all these steps share?

options.text_md: To move the capital to Delhi from Agra
To lower the rank of every noble
To build a stable empire in which many groups were bound to the emperor as loyal partners
To end all trade between regions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To build a stable empire in which many groups were bound to the emperor as loyal partners. Each step tied different groups and regions to the state through alliances, equal treatment in taxes, a common language of administration and a uniform system, which gave a stable empire with loyal allies. None of them moved a capital, lowered every noble's rank or stopped trade.

questions.stem_md: An imagined exhibition panel in Kota Gallery lists "Social reforms of Akbar, as commonly taught". Which entry belongs under this heading?

options.text_md: Discouraging forced sati and allowing widow remarriage
Fixing the zat and sawar of nobles
Building the Jama Masjid of Delhi

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Discouraging forced sati and allowing widow remarriage. Discouraging forced sati and allowing widow remarriage are among the social reforms commonly taught for Akbar. Zat and sawar belong to the mansabdari system, the token currency to Muhammad bin Tughlaq, and the Jama Masjid to Shah Jahan.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Principal of Shanti Niketan School says her school's new timetable is "in the spirit of Akbar's plan for schools". Which feature of his educational reform fits it best?

options.text_md: A ban on all schooling for girls and boys
Teaching only one language in every school
Closing every school at Fatehpur Sikri
Practical subjects such as mathematics, agriculture and history taught alongside the usual subjects

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Practical subjects such as mathematics, agriculture and history taught alongside the usual subjects. Akbar is commonly taught to have encouraged education with practical subjects such as mathematics, agriculture and history. He did not ban schooling or close schools.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined translation department of Fatehpur Sikri, a clerk is told to prepare a Persian version of the Mahabharata. By what name is this translation known?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Razmnama. The Persian translation of the Mahabharata is called the Razmnama. The Akbarnama is the history of Akbar's reign, the Baburnama is the memoir of Babur and the Ain-i-Akbari is its third part on administration.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Mughal records office of Class IX's project, a word is written on the file of each noble: "mansab". What does the word mansab mean?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rank. Mansab means rank. Land assigned as pay is a jagir, a tax is a revenue demand, and horsemen are counted under sawar.

questions.stem_md: The imagined mansabdar Nawab Rahim is entered in the register with a zat of 1,000 and a sawar of 500. What does the sawar of 500 tell us?

options.text_md: He is paid 500 rupees every year
He is the 500th noble in the list

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** He must maintain 500 horsemen. Sawar is the number of horsemen the officer must maintain, so 500 horsemen. His personal rank and pay are shown by his zat of 1,000, and the sawar figure is not a salary or a serial number.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined mansabdars of Akbar, one paid directly from the treasury and one given the revenue of villages near Shahpur, are discussed in class. In what two ways could mansabdars be paid?

options.text_md: In cash or by a gift of horses
By a jagir or by a share of trade
In cash or by a jagir
By land purchase or by loans

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** In cash or by a jagir. Payment was either in cash or by a jagir, which was an assignment of land revenue. Gifts of horses, a share of trade, land purchase and loans were not the ways of paying a mansabdar.

questions.stem_md: Nawab Farhan, an imagined mansabdar of Akbar, dies, and his son Anwar hopes to receive the same rank automatically. What does the mansabdari system say about this?

options.text_md: Ranks passed to the eldest son automatically
Ranks passed to the officer's brother
Ranks were sold to the highest bidder
Ranks were not hereditary, so the emperor decided whether to give Anwar a rank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Ranks were not hereditary, so the emperor decided whether to give Anwar a rank. Mansabs were not hereditary, so a son could not claim a father's rank as of right. The emperor decided, which also supported loyalty to him. Ranks were not passed on automatically and were not sold.

questions.stem_md: An imagined inspector at a muster near Bahadurpur finds that some of the horsemen shown on the roll are not present, and that some horses have been borrowed for the day. Which defect of the mansabdari system does this illustrate?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** False musters. Showing horsemen or horses that do not exist or are borrowed for the day is a false muster, a known defect. Ranks were not hereditary, payment was by cash or jagir, and Persian was the language of administration.

questions.stem_md: An imagined revenue note from late in the Mughal period says that many mansabdars had no jagirs to receive and that those who did often pressed the peasants hard. Which defect or defects of the system does it show?

options.text_md: The ranks being given on merit
The shortage of jagirs and pressure on peasants by jagirdars

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The shortage of jagirs and pressure on peasants by jagirdars. A shortage of jagirs and pressure on peasants by jagirdars are named defects, which grew when control weakened under later rulers. Ranks on merit, efficient control and loyalty are merits of the system.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Historians value the Ain-i-Akbari as a source, but read it with care.

**Reason (R):** It gives detailed official information, yet its author Abul Fazl was a courtier of Akbar and so wrote in praise of him.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

(ii) At the **Ibadat Khana** in **Fatehpur Sikri**, from about **1575**, scholars of different faiths met and discussed ideas. **Persian** was made the language of **administration**, so that officers in different regions used one language in their work.

(iii) Removing special levies treated subjects more alike in tax matters, and the Ibadat Khana gave scholars a place to exchange ideas. (i) As commonly taught, he **discouraged forced sati**, allowed **widow remarriage** and tried to discourage **child marriage** by fixing **minimum ages** for marriage.

(ii) He encouraged **education** by having practical subjects such as **mathematics, agriculture and history** taught in schools. His **translation department** had Sanskrit works, such as the **Mahabharata** (the **Razmnama**), and other works put into Persian, so that they could be read by officers and scholars who used that language.

(iii) He gave **patronage** to scholars, painters and musicians. The musician **Tansen** is a well-known example. With such support, painters and scholars worked at his court, which became a centre of art and learning in the empire.

(ii) Explain zat and sawar, the range of ranks and the ways of payment. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the rules that governed mansabdars. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and origin; zat, sawar, ranks and payment; rules.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Mansab** means **rank**. The system was introduced by **Akbar** about the **1570s** (dates vary).

(ii) **Zat** was the **personal rank and pay**, and **sawar** was the **number of horsemen** to be maintained. Ranks ranged from **10 up to 5,000** for nobles, and were higher for princes. Payment was in **cash** or by a **jagir**, an assignment of land revenue.

(iii) Ranks were **not hereditary**, so a son had no claim to a father's rank. Officers were **transferred**, and ranks were given on **merit**. The emperor could promote or demote, which kept officers loyal to him.

questions.stem_md:
Historians assess the mansabdari system by its merits and its defects.

(i) State three merits of the system. **[3]**
(ii) State three defects of the system. **[3]**
(iii) Give an overall assessment of the system, with a reason. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three merits; three defects; a reasoned overall assessment.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The system gave an **efficient army and administration**. Officers owed **loyalty to the emperor**. Ranks were given on **merit**, so able men could rise.

(ii) **False musters** showed horsemen or horses that were not really maintained. **Jagirdars** put **pressure on peasants**. Later there was a **shortage of jagirs**, and control became **weak under later rulers**.

(iii) On balance the system worked well while the emperor kept firm control, because officers were loyal and able men could rise through merit. It weakened when jagirs became scarce and checks on musters grew lax. So its success depended on strong supervision by the emperor, and its defects grew when that supervision weakened.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Shortage of jagirs and weak control later
(iii) Judgement that it worked under strong control
(iii) Reason: scarcity of jagirs and lax checks weakened it
